results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 49 unit summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph, in spec order; the three callout entries are not units.

results.draft_locus: The Unit Economics of an Order ¶2
results.finding: The spec's controlling idea unifies the two points (numbers that look like design and finance matters are architecture matters), but the paragraph's topic sentence announces two separate observations, so the reverse outliner read two ideas. A topic sentence naming the common idea would make it one.

Every unit traces to a supporting claim: scene to S1, models and public record to S2/S3, promise chain to S3, economics, worked example and peak to S3/S4, stages to S5, incidents and choices to S6; transitional units (p03, p06, p32a, p48) serve their sections and the conclusion synthesises the claims.

Every table is introduced by a sentence saying what it gives (models table, promise table with its last row, metrics table, worked table followed by 'Read across', stage definition, comparison table), every figure has an explanatory caption, and each quotation and statistic (Shopify GMV, Amazon seller of record, Nike, Marketplace Pulse, Census/Adobe/Shopify peak, Hobbycraft, vendor prices) is followed by what it shows.

results.quote: Online growth is now in single digits (Dutch online consumer spending fell 1% to €35.7 billion in 2025, per the Thuiswinkel Markt Monitor; German online goods sales rose 3.2% to €83.1 billion, per bevh), so Omnichannel merchants compete on margin, returns and operations.
results.finding: The section's transition_in carries over 'the Omnichannel stage, where the joins between systems become the problem', but the boundary opens on market statistics; the joins are reached only in the third sentence, so the example relationship to the preceding stage discussion is not expressed at the boundary.

All other declared transitions (introduction, scene, models, public record, promise chain, economics, worked example, peak, stages, incidents, choices, conclusion and hand-off) express their relationship at the boundary and pick up what carries_over names.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶1
results.quote: The definitions above come from reports, and the four lines from one fictional company.
results.finding: Both readers found the public-record section interrupts the move from what the models are to what they change, and both proposed placing it after the promise chain; reader B called its position partly unclear. The difficulty is the declared section order (which a previous round set), not the prose.
results.corroborated_by: cold_flow_B, point 2 ('In Practice ... Partly unclear') and point 4 ('Move "In Practice"')

results.draft_locus: The Business Models, Defined by the People Who Report Them ¶3
results.quote: Kestrel & Pine runs four at once: D2C, online and in its own stores; wholesale; marketplace selling; and, where stores and web shop share stock and orders, omnichannel.
results.finding: The four lines (online, wholesale, stores, marketplace) do not map onto the four models named here, nor onto the five promise-table columns or the three worked-example lines; both readers stopped to reconcile the store's status.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶2
results.quote: Stores are the larger channel, and the architecture must treat them as one.
results.finding: 'Treat them as one' is ambiguous (as one channel, or as one with online); both readers re-read it.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶5
results.quote: US figures are measured differently: Forrester's older 2022 forecast expected B2B e-commerce to reach about $3 trillion by 2027 and tracked EDI separately, at about a fifth of all US business-to-business transactions, large enough to be counted on its own.
results.finding: The Forrester sentence is convoluted and muddies the EU point; both readers re-read it.

results.quote: Online growth is now in single digits (Dutch online consumer spending fell 1% to €35.7 billion in 2025, per the Thuiswinkel Markt Monitor; German online goods sales rose 3.2% to €83.1 billion, per bevh), so Omnichannel merchants compete on margin, returns and operations.
results.finding: Both readers found the market statistic a weak bridge from the hubs to the incidents and paused to find the link to unowned shared facts; the prose can make the link explicit within the spec's declared opening.
results.corroborated_by: cold_flow_B, point 3 ('Opening of "When It Goes Wrong"')

results.draft_locus: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶2
results.quote: That is an order management decision at national scale, though Target does not name its system.
results.finding: Order management (OMS, on does_not_know) is used here before it is defined in the stage table five sections later; both readers flagged it.
Opens on a concrete case (one jacket sold to a shopper and to a retail chain), not a placeholder, restated question, definition, sweeping history or book report.
Opens with a callback and synthesis, then sorted take-aways and questions; no 'in conclusion' opener, no new subtopic, not the thesis merely rephrased.

'What to Take Away' ¶1 joins models, facts versus promises and stages into the answer to the share-or-separate question, and the author's synthesis says the promise table and unit-economics table show where the architecture must be strong; refusing a copied architecture is carried by question 8.
'The chapter opened with one jacket sold twice ...' returns to the opening sale and says what the software lacked: shared facts are fine, each promise kept at its own edge.

The cold reader predicted the main claim and the section order (scene, models, public record, promise chain, economics with jacket and peak, stages, failures, share-or-separate answer) in line with the roadmap; the choices section is predicted as the closing question.

Reader placed the brand in Growing, close to the move into Omnichannel, argued from channels, models and stock locations and explicitly not from revenue; this matches the expected 'moving from Growing to Omnichannel'. The spec's open question on rewording the expected answer stands.
Marketplace captures (seller imports), seller sets price under parity rules, seller is seller of record, seller holds stock and ships: all five match.
Return rate pulls on the reverse flow designed across systems, not bolted on; the peak pulls on capacity of the whole chain including integrations, not only the storefront.
Reader recommends moving to the shared core at the second-writer trigger, shares product, price list, stock and order record, keeps each line's promises at its edge, and rejects a stack per line.
